lead: A diode rectifier gives one fixed DC voltage. Replace the diodes with thyristors and you can delay every turn-on by a firing angle α. The average output then follows a cosine of α: full positive at α = 0, zero at 90°, and negative beyond 90° if the current keeps flowing. Battery chargers, DC motor drives and electrolysis supplies work this way: a gate pulse worth milliwatts controls kilowatts of DC. This chapter covers the single-phase half-wave, half-controlled and fully controlled circuits with R and RL loads, and the difference between continuous and discontinuous current.
prereq: You need: SCR turn-on and natural commutation (Unit 1, Power Semiconductor Devices), and the diode circuits of 2.1, which are this chapter at α = 0.

sections.h3: The firing angle sets the start of conduction

blocks.text: A diode conducts the instant the supply forward-biases it. A thyristor waits for a gate pulse at ωt = α. The firing angle α, in degrees, is measured from the natural firing point: the instant the same device would start conducting if it were a diode. Never measure it from the supply zero crossing. Natural commutation is the later instant when the device current reaches zero and it turns off; in the bridge circuits here the two instants coincide.
Half-wave controlled rectifier: one SCR fed by vs = Vm sin ωt, where Vm is the peak supply voltage in volts. The SCR conducts from α to π, then blocks, so:

blocks.where: Vdc is the average load voltage in volts; Vm is the peak supply voltage in volts; α is the firing angle in degrees.

blocks.text: At α = 0 this is Vm/π, the diode half-wave value. With a pure resistance the current is discontinuous at every α: it reaches zero at π and stays there until the next pulse.

Add inductance and the current cannot stop at π. Energy stored in L drives it on to ωt = β, the extinction angle, where the current reaches zero. Between π and β the supply is already negative while the current is still positive, so the output has a negative part and Vdc falls below the resistance value:

blocks.where: β is the extinction angle in degrees, between π and π + α. As β grows over that range, Vdc falls from the resistance value (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α) to (Vm/π)cos α.

blocks.text: With enough inductance the current never stops; conduction is then continuous and Vdc = (Vm/π)cos α, which is negative for α > 90°. Half-wave circuits push DC through the transformer and appear only in small, cheap supplies.
With a back EMF E in the load, conduction can start only once vs exceeds E, so the SCR fires at ωt = sin⁻¹(E/Vm) + α.

sections.h3: Fully controlled bridge: four thyristors, two pulses

blocks.text: Four SCRs in a bridge. T1 and T2 form one diagonal pair and are fired at α; T3 and T4 at α + 180°. Each pair conducts for half a cycle, so the output has two pulses per supply cycle and its ripple sits at 2f, that is 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply. Each device blocks Vm in reverse.

blocks.where: 2Vm/π is the highest average available, 0.6366 Vm; on a 230 V supply Vm = 325.3 V, so the ceiling is 207.1 V. The range runs from +207 V through zero at α = 90° down to −207 V.

blocks.text: With a pure resistance the current stops at π, so only the positive part of each pulse survives: Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α), always positive and zero only at α = 180°. Conduction is continuous when the load inductance carries current past the next firing instant; otherwise it is discontinuous, conduction ends at an extinction angle before the next firing instant, and the actual Vdc is higher than the continuous-current formula predicts (for example (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) against (2Vm/π)cos α).

Above α = 90° the cosine formula gives a negative Vdc. That is real only if current can keep flowing the same way: an RL load, or an RLE load whose back EMF is more negative than the average output (its magnitude is larger), so the load itself drives the current round in the same direction. Power then flows from the DC side into the AC supply. This is inverter mode, the two-quadrant operation of 2.7. A pure resistor cannot do it, because a thyristor conducts one way only.

sections.h3: Half-controlled bridge and the freewheeling diode

blocks.text: The half-controlled (semi) bridge replaces two SCRs with diodes. When the supply voltage tries to reverse across the load, the diodes conduct and hold the output at zero, so Vdc never goes negative. For both R and RL loads Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α). The gate drive is simpler and the input power factor at a given α is better, but inversion is impossible: one quadrant only.

A freewheeling diode across the load does the same job inside a fully controlled bridge. Connect its cathode to the positive rail. The moment the bridge output tries to go negative, the diode conducts and the load current freewheels through it; the load sees zero instead of a negative voltage, so Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α). The energy in L is not returned to the supply, which raises the displacement factor (see 2.5), but the supply current now flows in short blocks.

figure.caption: Only the continuous-current curve crosses zero and turns negative; the resistance curves stay positive and reach zero only at 180 degrees.

spec.aria: Three cosine-shaped curves of normalised average output against firing angle, the continuous-current curve passing through zero at 90 degrees.

examples.question: A single-phase fully controlled bridge works from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply with a load resistance R = 10 Ω. Find Vdc and Idc at α = 60° (a) for continuous current, (b) for the pure resistance load. Comment on the difference.
steps: Comment: the resistance load conducts only from 60° to 180° of each half cycle, so no negative part appears and the average is 50 % higher. The continuous-current result needs enough inductance to keep current flowing; with only 10 Ω it cannot be reached.
examples.answer: With continuous current Vdc = 103.54 V and Idc = 10.35 A; with the pure resistance load Vdc = 155.31 V and Idc = 15.53 A.
examples.check:
import math
Vm = 230*math.sqrt(2)
print(round(Vm, 2))
print(round(2*Vm/math.pi, 2))
a = math.radians(60)
Vdc_c = (2*Vm/math.pi)*math.cos(a)
print(round(Vdc_c, 2))
print(round(Vdc_c/10, 2))
Vdc_d = (Vm/math.pi)*(1+math.cos(a))
print(round(Vdc_d, 2))
print(round(Vdc_d/10, 2))

examples.question: The same bridge feeds an RL load with enough inductance for continuous current at α = 120°. Find Vdc and say what it means.
steps: The negative sign means the DC terminals deliver power back to the AC supply: inverter mode. Current still flows in one direction through the load, so the load must supply or store energy.
examples.answer: Vdc = −103.54 V, so the converter runs in inverter mode and returns 103.54 × Idc watts to the AC side.

traps: Using Vdc = (2Vm/π)cos α on a pure resistance load. That formula needs continuous current; with R the correct one is (Vm/π)(1 + cos α).
Measuring α from the supply zero crossing when the load has a back EMF E. The SCR can start only once vs exceeds E, so the reference has already moved by sin⁻¹(E/Vm) and α adds to it.
Reporting a negative Vdc for a half-controlled bridge. Its diodes clamp the output at zero; only the fully controlled bridge inverts.
Forgetting that inversion needs a current path. With a pure resistor the current cannot reverse and Vdc stays at or above zero, whatever the formula suggests.
Losing the factor of two between the half-wave value (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α) and the bridge value (Vm/π)(1 + cos α).

quiz.q: Define firing angle and natural firing point for a single-phase controlled rectifier.
quiz.a: The firing angle α is the delay in degrees from the natural firing point to the instant the gate pulse is applied. The natural firing point is the instant the device would start conducting if it were a diode. Natural commutation is the later instant when its current falls to zero and it turns off.

quiz.q: Why does the half-controlled bridge never give a negative average output?
quiz.a: Its two diodes conduct as soon as the supply voltage tries to reverse across the load, holding the output at zero and carrying the load current. The output therefore has no negative part, so the average can only fall to zero at α = 180°.

quiz.q: A half-wave controlled rectifier runs from 230 V, 50 Hz with R = 20 Ω and α = 45°. Find Vdc and Idc.
A fully controlled bridge with continuous current works at α = 120° from a 230 V supply. Find Vdc.
quiz.a: 2Vm/π = 207.07 V, Vdc = 207.07 × cos 120° = −103.54 V. The converter is in inverter mode and returns power to the AC side.

quiz.q: What does a freewheeling diode change in a fully controlled bridge with an RL load, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: It conducts when the output would go negative, clamping the load voltage at zero, so Vdc becomes (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) instead of (2Vm/π)cos α. Inductor energy stays in the load, so the displacement factor improves. The cost is that supply current becomes discontinuous and the load current ripple pattern changes.

quiz.q: For a fixed α and a fixed supply, what decides whether the current is continuous?
quiz.a: Whether the load inductance keeps current flowing up to the next firing instant. A large ωL/R (long load time constant) or a large back EMF keeps it continuous; a pure resistance never is. Below the boundary the continuous-current formula under-predicts Vdc, because the discontinuous output is higher (less negative in inverter mode), and the actual value must be found from the extinction angle.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phase-controlled line-commutated converters remain the workhorse of high-voltage DC transmission and large DC drives, but new designs increasingly use PWM active front ends, which shape the input current into a sine and give a displacement factor near unity. The same cosine law reappears in cycloconverters and in the grid-side converter of a solar inverter, where firing angle becomes a modulation index. Look up line-commutated converter, extinction angle control, and HVDC firing-angle control if you want to go further.
